item.subject: Mathematics
item.stem:
Geometry Tiles
Instruction:

For this item, you have been given a piece of cardboard with 6 tiles like the ones shown below. Take the piece of cardboard, and punch out the 6 tiles.

If you do not have the piece of cardboard, raise your hand.

4 Triangle Tiles
[Image: Four triangle tiles]

2 Trapezoid Tiles
[Image: Two trapezoid tiles]

These tiles can be used to make new figures. One problem has been done for you

USE: 3 Triangle Tiles
MAKE: A trapezoid
SHOW: Draw it on the grid.
[Image: Example showing a trapezoid drawn on the grid]

Now try these problems.

A.

USE: 1 Triangle Tile and
1 Trapezoid Tile
MAKE: A 4-sided figure
SHOW: Draw it on the grid.

[Image: Triangular grid]

descriptors:
Correct 4-sided figure turned in any position
[Image: A parallelogram composed of one trapezoid tile and one triangle tile]
Makes a larger triangle
Makes a 4-sided figure, but not using the specified tiles, e.g., a larger parallelogram.
Other incorrect (including crossed out, erased, stray marks, illegible, or off task)
Blank

item.figure_description:
The stem includes four diagrams:
1. '4 Triangle Tiles': Four identical equilateral triangles of unit side length, arranged in a row pointing alternately up, down, up, and down.
2. '2 Trapezoid Tiles': Two identical isosceles trapezoids each composed of three equilateral triangle units (bottom base 2 units, top base 1 unit, legs 1 unit for the first one; and inverted with top base 2 units, bottom base 1 unit for the second one).
3. Worked example grid: An isometric grid forming a parallelogram with horizontal top and bottom sides of 3 units each and slanted sides of 2 units each, divided by dashed lines into 2 rows of 6 equilateral triangles. In the top-right portion, a trapezoid made of 3 triangle units (top side 1 unit, bottom side 2 units, slanted sides 1 unit) is outlined in bold solid lines.
4. Part A response grid: An identical empty parallelogram-shaped isometric grid with top and bottom edges of 3 units, slanted sides of 2 units, divided into 2 rows of 6 equilateral triangle units by dashed lines.
item.calibration: Concurrent calibration of the TIMSS 2003 data, 2007 bridging data, and 2007 data (fourth-grade mathematics).

reference_items.figure_description:
At the top is an equilateral triangle with dots at each of its three vertices, labeled "tile" to the right of its right edge.

Below is an irregular polygon drawn on an isometric (triangular) dot grid, with dots marking vertices along its boundary and in its interior:
- Top edge: a horizontal segment 3 units long, with 4 dots evenly spaced (including endpoints).
- Left boundary: from the top-left dot, a line goes down and right by 1 unit to an indented vertex dot; from there, a line goes down and left by 1 unit to the bottom-left corner dot.
- Bottom edge: a horizontal segment 4 units long, with 5 dots evenly spaced (including endpoints).
- Right boundary: from the top-right dot, a line goes down and right by 1 unit to a vertex dot at the middle horizontal level; from that dot, a horizontal line extends right by 1 unit to another vertex dot; from that dot, a line goes down and left by 1 unit to the bottom-right corner dot.
- Interior: 2 dots are spaced along the middle horizontal level between the left indented vertex and the right boundary.

reference_items.stem:
[Image: six pieces of cardboard with length of the sides labeled in cm. Two of the pieces are square shaped with each side measured at 1 cm. Four of the pieces are rectangular shaped with two sides measured at 1 cm and two other sides measured at 2 cm.]

Susan has the 6 pieces of cardboard shown above. Which of the following shapes could Susan make using all 6 of these pieces without cutting them?
reference_items.figure_description:
At the top of the item, six gray-shaded flat cardboard shapes are shown. Two are identical squares, each labeled '1 cm' on all four sides (top, bottom, left, and right). Four are identical horizontal rectangles, each labeled '2 cm' on the top and bottom sides and '1 cm' on the left and right sides.

The response options show line drawings of four 3D geometric solids with dashed lines representing hidden edges:
- Option A: A cube.
- Option B: A triangular prism resting on one of its rectangular faces.
- Option C: A truncated pyramid with a square or rectangular base and top.
- Option D: A tall right rectangular prism standing on a square base.
reference_items.calibration: Concurrent calibration of the TIMSS 2007 and 2011 fourth-grade mathematics data.

reference_items.figure_description: At the top of the item is a solid black equilateral triangle with a horizontal base and its apex pointing directly upward. Below the question is an outline of a concave seven-sided polygon (heptagon) composed of five contiguous equilateral triangles of the same size as the tile above. The polygon has a horizontal bottom edge. From each end of the bottom edge, a side edge angles upward and outward at 60 degrees. From these two outer vertices, two edges angle upward and inward at 60 degrees to form two top peaks. From each top peak, an edge angles downward at 60 degrees toward the center, meeting in an interior V-shaped notch located at the center of what would otherwise be a regular hexagon.

slope.instructions: TIMSS scaled this 1-point item with the two-parameter logistic (2PL) model, which TIMSS uses for constructed-response items worth 1 point, in the calibration "Concurrent calibration of the TIMSS 2003 data, 2007 bridging data, and 2007 data (fourth-grade mathematics)". What is the item's slope (discrimination) parameter a? A higher a means that the item separates students of lower and higher mathematics ability more sharply. Choose the value closest to it. The state also lists reference items: the calibrated TIMSS items of the same grade most similar to this one (never the item itself or its other parts), most similar first, with their percent correct and their calibrated parameters, each on the scale of its own calibration. Use them to place this item.
